notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense makes Cassandra's warning vivid, even though no one listens.

notes.label: Framing word order
notes.body: fatis and futuris frame the line around Cassandra herself, so she is surrounded by the doom she foresees.

notes.label: Emphatic negative
notes.body: non umquam ("not ever") is stronger than a simple "never", which stresses the cruelty of her curse.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: Apollo granted Cassandra the ability to predict the future to convince her to sleep with him, when she changed her mind, he cursed her to never be believed.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: nos opens the line and miseri comes later, so Aeneas lingers over the pitiful picture of his people.

notes.label: Pathos
notes.body: Aeneas calls his people "wretched", looking back with the knowledge of what was to come, so the reader feels his grief.

notes.label: Superlative
notes.body: It was Troy's last day, yet the Trojans celebrate it: a sharp dramatic irony.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense shows the festive garlands being hung, which makes the irony more painful.

notes.label: Framing word order
notes.body: festa and fronde frame the verb, so the garlands seem to wrap around the whole action.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The phrase ends the sentence, stressing that the whole city is celebrating its own destruction.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: Opening with "turns" marks a change of time and scene: the day is over.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense makes nightfall feel immediate and threatening.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The verb comes before its subject, so night seems to rush in suddenly.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense makes the coming of night swift and dramatic.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: nox ends the line with a single heavy syllable, so darkness falls with a thud.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The participle opens the line, so we feel the night wrapping everything up before we learn what it covers.

notes.label: Variatio
notes.body: Virgil uses two different words for the sky, which avoids repetition and makes the darkness seem to fill the whole heavens.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: dolos ends its phrase, so the Greek trickery is the last thing the night covers: it hides the danger along with everything else.

notes.label: Enjambment
notes.body: The verb is carried over to the final line, which brings the passage to rest. It also echoes conticuere, the first word of Book 2, closing the set text with a ring.

notes.label: Framing word order
notes.body: fessos and artus frame sleep's embrace, so sleep wraps around the Trojans just as the snakes wrapped around Laocoön.

notes.label: The Trojans
notes.body: The Teucri are the Trojans, named after Teucer, one of the first kings of Troy.

notes.label: Festive garlands
notes.body: Hanging leafy garlands on temples was what people did at festivals of thanksgiving. The Trojans believe the war is over and are giving thanks to the gods.

notes.label: The Myrmidons
notes.trans: and the tricks of the Myrmidons
notes.body: The Myrmidons were Achilles' soldiers, led at Troy after his death by his son Neoptolemus. Here they stand for the Greeks in general, hidden in the horse.

questions: How does Virgil make the Trojans' celebrations seem tragic in lines 248–249?
How does the description of nightfall in lines 250–253 build tension?
Looking back over the whole set text, who or what is most to blame for the fall of Troy: the Greeks, the gods, or the Trojans themselves?
How does Virgil make us sympathise with the Trojans even as they make terrible mistakes?

context.body:
The set text ends with Troy asleep. Later that night the Greek fleet sails back from the island of Tenedos, where it had been hiding, and Sinon lets the Greek warriors out of the horse. They kill the guards and open the gates to their army.

The ghost of Hector appears to Aeneas in a dream and tells him to flee and take Troy's gods with him. Aeneas fights at first, but after seeing King Priam killed he escapes, carrying his old father Anchises on his shoulders and leading his young son Ascanius by the hand. His wife Creusa is lost in the confusion, and her ghost tells him of the new home that awaits him in the west.
